newsitem.title: NORWAY: Red Cross wants world watchdog on weapons markets.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross wants world watchdog on weapons markets.

text.p: The president of the International Committee of the Red Cross, concerned about attacks on aid workers, called on Friday for global controls on the conventional weapons trade.

Cornelio Sommaruga also said the protection by armed guards of ICRC premises and warehouses might be intensified as a measure against looting by bandits. But armed escorts of convoys were counter-productive and could draw more fire, he said.

"I think it is urgent that we place another issue on our agenda of priorities, namely the introduction of a system for controlling legal and illegal weapons transfers and markets," Sommaruga told a meeting on challenges to humanitarian work organised by the Norwegian Red Cross.
The ICRC lost six Western employees in Chechnya -- including two Norwegian women -- and another three in Burundi in attacks last year, the highest number of such deaths in its 133-year history.

The six medical staff in Chechnya were shot dead by gunmen in December as they slept in a hospital compound, prompting the ICRC to pull out of the troubled region. Three Swiss staff were killed in an ambush last June in Burundi.

"The weapons which are killing humanitarian workers are Kalashnikovs, mines, all those small weapons," Sommaruga told reporters after the speech. "You have weapons on all sides. Weapons are getting into the refugee camps. Where are all these weapons coming from?"
The ICRC, with more than 8,000 workers, takes a leading role in enforcing international law governing the use of weapons in war, treatment of prisoners and civilians.

It looks after the sick, visits prisoners, feeds the hungry and saves lives in flashpoints from east Zaire, Rwanda and Somalia to ex-Yugoslavia and Afghanistan. Its humanitarian work depends on its neutrality and fragile trust.
Sommaruga said looting was a problem in addition to attacks.
"We have already had, for some years, guards looking after our premises," he said, but added that armed protection of aid workers on the move had turned out to be a bad experience.
Faced with the urgent needs of starving civilians in Somalia, the ICRC took the exceptional decision to place its convoys under the protection of armed militias.
"It was very counter-productive because finally we may have been attacked simply because we had armed guards," he said. "Resorting to military protection has its limits."
An estimated 300,000 people died in the famine which devastated Somalia between 1991 and late 1992.

"The only real course open to humanitarian action, and it is the option we have chosen, is to work tirelessly and resolutely to restore and demand respect for the protective Red Cross and Red Crescent emblems," Sommaruga said in his speech.
Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal said: "Victims of war have a right to receive assistance and aid workers have a right to deliver such assistance safely.
"We demand that those who commit crimes against aid workers are apprehended, tried in a court of law and punished. This is a struggle we cannot afford to lose," Godal told the conference.
